item.title: Geoeconomics and the Great Power Struggle for Eurasia
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Eurasian integration aims to alter the balance of power and undermine the foundations of US global primacy. The world’s largest continent in terms of landmass, natural resources and population has historically been divided by conflicts, a lack of shared infrastructure and insufficient mechanisms for cooperation. Limited economic connectivity among land powers has given maritime powers a competitive advantage in controlling the main transportation corridors. In the language of Halford Mackinder and Nicholas Spykman, the divisions in Europe and the wider Eurasian supercontinent (from the Atlantic to the Pacific) have enabled maritime powers to exercise control from the periphery or ‘rimland’. While maritime powers have historically sought to enhance their power by keeping Eurasia divided, the Eurasian land powers seek to strengthen themselves by developing greater economic connectivity. However, economic integration must be based on what I term a ‘balance of dependence’ to prevent the emergence of a new hegemon.

Geoeconomics and the ‘balance of dependence’

Geoeconomics entails state intervention into the market to procure a privileged economic position, while the resulting economic instruments of power are utilised to extract political power. As Edward Luttwak argued, geoeconomics employs ‘the logic of war in the grammar of commerce’.

The ‘balance of dependence’ is the geoeconomic equivalent of the military balance of power, as the less dependent state can extract political concessions from the more dependent state. States therefore seek to enhance their bargaining power by reducing their own dependence through diversifying economic partnerships and developing strategic industries, while increasing the dependence of others. A balance of dependence encourages stable and mutually beneficial cooperation, as neither side can exercise economic coercion without inflicting significant costs on itself.

A common theme in international political economy is the enduring dilemma between recognising that prosperity and influence necessitate integration into the global economy, and the ambition of states to maintain economic and political autonomy. Yet, there is no inherent contradiction between these two objectives since power derives from the ability of states to manipulate the symmetry within interdependent relationships. Minimise your own dependence on others, while enhance their reliance on you.

Building on the work of Albert Hirschman, economic interdependence through the prism of power competition can be broken down into the ‘positive’ aspect of gaining influence over others as they become dependent, and the ‘negative’ aspect of losing autonomy as other states gain influence. Asymmetrical dependence empowers the less dependent state to set favourable economic conditions and extract political concessions.

Rational states will therefore seek to diversify economic partnerships, control strategic industries and develop favourable value-chains, transportation corridors, financial institutions, trade currencies and trading blocs.

Economic coercion is only sustainable when used in moderation as excessive use increases the incentives for weaker states to reduce their dependence. The advantage of the weaker and more dependent state is its willingness to accept significant economic pain to obtain greater autonomy. Economic sanctions are thus a very risky geoeconomic gamble that can undermine the economic foundations from which political power is derived. This reality was obscured during the unipolar moment in the 1990s and onward as there were no real alternatives.

The illusion of the free market

What is good for the free market is not necessarily good for the state. A company may increase its profits by moving production abroad, while the state loses its industrial base, technological expertise and economic independence. Governments must therefore ensure that the economy serves the strategic interests of the state.

The advocacy of free trade has historically been motivated more by power interests than by economic principles. The German economist Friedrich List argued that Britain had become the dominant economic power in the world by protecting its industries, intervening in the economy and controlling the seas. Once Britain had established its economic supremacy, it had much to gain from free trade as other countries could not compete with British industries. Land powers were also less enthusiastic about free trade as they would become dependent on trade routes controlled by their rivals. List thus denounced the British advocacy of free trade as an effort to ‘kick away the ladder’ by which Britain had climbed to greatness.

The US similarly grew throughout the 19th century based on the principles of the American System, in which it sought economic sovereignty from Britain to ensure its political sovereignty. Yet, after the US gained a dominant position, it also kicked away the ladder. The same logic prevailed after the Cold War. The West had much to gain from opening up the economies of the former communist states to Western companies. Despite the economic success of East Asian countries that had relied heavily on government intervention, the West promoted free-market capitalism as the universal formula for economic development.

Why states organise themselves into economic blocs

Much like states join military alliances to enhance their security, they join economic blocs to enhance their bargaining power. European integration was partly motivated by the ambition to negotiate with the US on more equal terms. The emergence of powerful trading blocs in Europe and North America similarly created incentives for the countries of Asia to organise themselves into larger economic regions.

There is an apparent contradiction in the relationship between economic integration and national sovereignty. Smaller countries surrender some sovereignty by joining an economic bloc, yet membership can also strengthen their sovereignty by making their economies more competitive and reducing their dependence on outside powers.

However, there must also be a balance of dependence within an economic bloc. If the most powerful country abuses its dominant position to extract political concessions from the smaller member states, the latter will have an interest in developing economic partnerships outside the bloc. This is especially a challenge for both the EU and Russian-led integration projects.

The struggle for Eurasia

The demise of the Mongol Empire disrupted the trade routes connecting the major civilisations of Eurasia. The Europeans subsequently sought to establish maritime trade routes to reach the wealthy markets of Asia. This marked the beginning of 500 years of Western dominance as the main trade routes, resources, technologies and financial institutions gradually came under the control of Western powers.

The British geographer Halford Mackinder warned already in 1904 that the advantage of maritime powers could come to an end. The construction of Russian railways across the Eurasian supercontinent would enable the land powers to trade with each other without relying on the seas controlled by Britain. Yet, Mackinder’s predictions did not materialise as communism and the Cold War prevented the major Eurasian powers from developing close economic relations.

The US inherited the role of Britain as the dominant maritime power, with a similar interest in keeping the major Eurasian land powers divided. American influence over Eurasia has largely been exercised from the periphery of the continent, through its allies in Europe and East Asia and its presence in the Middle East.

Mackinder feared that Russia could become the dominant power in the world by uniting Eurasia under its control. With the rise of Asia, it is unlikely that any one country could dominate the continent. Rather, Russia, China, Iran and India have a common interest in developing economic ties that reduce their dependence on the US.

The ambition to restore the ancient Silk Road entails much more than building railways, roads and pipelines. The Eurasian powers also develop their own technological partnerships, banks, payment systems, trading arrangements, industries and currencies.

Economic interdependence has not put an end to the rivalry between great powers, although it has changed the instruments with which they compete. The more the US uses economic coercion as an instrument to contain Russia, China and other rising powers, the greater their incentives to develop alternative economic partnerships. Today, China is shifting the balance of dependence by reducing its reliance on the US-led international economic architecture. China pursues technological leadership, industrial leadership, energy autonomy, new forms of physical connectivity across the world through the Belt and Road Initiative, and new financial instruments of power. Russia and other Eurasian powers are following China’s lead with similar initiatives on a smaller scale. These initiatives bear a striking resemblance to the American System, in which the US sought to establish its own manufacturing base, roads and ports, and a national bank to reduce its dependence on a dominant Britain.

Mackinder’s prediction of a shift in global power from the seas to the Eurasian landmass may thus finally materialise, more than a century.

item.title: Mike Benz: How NGOs and the CIA Hijacked Ukraine
item.description: Mike Benz, a former Deputy Assistant Secretary at the US State Department and executive director of the Foundation for Freedom Online, argues that American intelligence agencies have transformed non-governmental organizations into instruments of foreign political control, using them to influence governments, manipulate civil society, and subordinate Ukraine’s sovereignty to Western geopolitical and financial interests.
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Mike Benz, a former Deputy Assistant Secretary at the US State Department and executive director of the Foundation for Freedom Online, argues that American intelligence agencies have transformed non-governmental organizations into instruments of foreign political control, using them to influence governments, manipulate civil society, and subordinate Ukraine’s sovereignty to Western geopolitical and financial interests. This article is based on a transcript from an interview one year ago:

From CIA Covert Operations to NGO Influence

The relationship between American intelligence and civil society emerged during World War II, when the Office of Strategic Services established partnerships with churches, trade unions, and media organizations. These relationships continued under the CIA during the Cold War, becoming instruments for influencing political developments across Europe, Latin America, Africa, and Asia.

The CIA’s interference in Italy’s 1948 election demonstrated how media organizations, unions, and religious institutions could be mobilized to secure favorable political outcomes. However, revelations about intelligence operations during the 1960s and 1970s produced congressional investigations and restrictions on covert activities.

The Reagan administration responded by transferring many traditional CIA functions into ostensibly independent organizations, particularly the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), established in 1983.

NED provided a mechanism for financing political parties, labor unions, media outlets, and civil society organizations without the reputational damage associated with direct CIA involvement. Its bipartisan structure ensured support from both major American political parties, while its activities maintained close connections with the intelligence establishment.

The fundamental principle was straightforward: governments possessed financial resources but lacked credibility, while civil society possessed credibility but lacked funding. Financing NGOs allowed Washington to advance government objectives through organizations perceived as independent.

Ukraine’s Civil Society Under Foreign Control

Ukraine became a central target of this system following independence. NED, USAID, and associated organizations supported political movements, media institutions, and civil society networks involved in both the Orange Revolution and the 2014 Maidan uprising.

These operations extended beyond electoral politics. American funding penetrated Ukrainian journalism, education, cultural institutions, and public administration. Media organizations dependent on USAID funding could be subjected to external influence over editorial priorities and personnel. Educational initiatives sought to eliminate favorable interpretations of Ukraine’s historical relationship with Russia, while cultural programs promoted a European identity detached from the country’s shared Russian heritage.

Financial dependence also extended into government operations, including salaries and pensions. Such arrangements created political loyalty through economic necessity rather than persuasion alone. Ukraine’s formal independence therefore concealed extensive foreign influence over its domestic institutions.

The Economic Interests Behind Western Intervention

Ukraine’s transformation also served powerful Western financial interests. George Soros and major Western energy corporations sought opportunities arising from the privatization of Ukrainian industries and the displacement of Russian natural gas.

Companies including Chevron, Shell, and ExxonMobil pursued substantial Ukrainian energy investments. Removing Russian gas from European markets would create profitable opportunities for more expensive liquefied natural gas supplied by American and other Western producers.

The Soros network illustrates the convergence of financial speculation, political influence, and American foreign policy. Close relationships between investment interests, intelligence institutions, and government officials allow private financial actors to benefit from geopolitical transformations that their political networks help facilitate. American foreign policy increasingly serves these concentrated financial interests rather than ordinary American citizens.

How Zelensky’s Peace Mandate Was Neutralized by NGOs

The clearest demonstration of NGO power came after Volodymyr Zelensky’s landslide victory in the 2019 election. Zelensky received an overwhelming electoral mandate on a platform promising peace with Russia and a settlement in Donbass. Yet within weeks, approximately 70 Ukrainian NGOs and media organizations issued a memorandum establishing political red lines. The Ukraine Crisis Media Center, supported by the US State Department, USAID, NATO, and associated contractors, participated in this initiative.

The memorandum opposed independent negotiations with Russia (without NATO and the EU), compromises over territorial disputes, reconsideration of NATO and EU integration, relaxation of sanctions, challenges to IMF agreements, and revisions to Russian-language policies. The warning or threat was that crossing these boundaries would produce political instability amounted to a threat of another externally supported political upheaval. The organizations presenting themselves as Ukrainian civil society were financially dependent on the very Western institutions whose interests their demands protected.

The Destruction of Democratic Sovereignty

Ukraine’s experience demonstrates how foreign-funded NGOs can override democratic elections without formally abolishing electoral institutions. Citizens can elect a president (not at the moment), but the acceptable boundaries of government policy are established by external financial, diplomatic, and security networks.

The same machinery has also operated against American political figures threatening established foreign policy priorities, particularly Donald Trump and his proposals to reduce confrontation with Russia. The essential problem is the merger of intelligence operations, private financial interests, and supposedly independent civil society. Restoring democratic sovereignty requires dismantling this system of influence and ending the use of American foreign policy as an instrument of private enrichment.

item.title: The Death of Academic Freedom in Norway
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Norway’s largest print newspaper, Aftenposten, argued this week that I should not be allowed to teach at a Norwegian university. Why? They accuse me of lying and spreading conspiracy theories. Do they need any evidence for this character assassination? None at all. Instead, they attempt to justify it by comparing me to a Holocaust denier for no apparent reason. This is the new standard of journalism in Norway: journalists cite the smears of their colleagues and refer to government “fact-checks” that they cannot / refuse to defend. As they cannot find any incorrect facts, they have to accuse me of spreading a “narrative” similar to the Kremlin, or being “pro-Russian” as I argue for diplomacy instead of sending more Ukrainians to their deaths in a proxy war against the world’s largest nuclear power. There is nothing that can be done. They can make any absurd claims because nobody will come to your defence for fear of being caught in the line of fire. When the political-media establishment comes for you, you are truly all alone.

And why should I not be allowed to teach in Norway? I previously taught Russian security strategy, military studies, international relations theory, and political economy for nine years in Australia and Russia. However, I would never even consider teaching a class in Norway in which I had to mention the word “Russia,” as journalists would inevitably find something that deviates from NATO’s official truths and could thus be labelled as “Russian propaganda.” During my first year teaching in Norway, I was contacted by a Norwegian journalist investigating me for spreading Russian propaganda in the classroom. The allegations were easily dismissed, as I was teaching research methods and had never mentioned the word “Russia” in the classroom. For the past six and a half years, I have been teaching sociology and research methods, as it is difficult for Norwegian journalists to cancel someone for spreading “Russian propaganda” when they are teaching Max Weber and Émile Durkheim.

Ignoring inquiries?

The newspaper also had the audacity to write: “The professor largely ignores inquiries from mainstream Norwegian media outlets.” Absolute nonsense. What inquiries have I ever received from Norwegian journalists? Over the past 6.5 years, I have been contacted approximately 25-30 times to respond to accusations of being “controversial”, “pro-Russian”, “pro-Georgian”, “pro-Iranian”, “pro-Chinese”, a “propagandist”, or “spreading Kremlin narratives”. My engagement with the media has been reduced to being allowed to respond to smears and labels that are never backed up by any evidence. Consequently, every media inquiry produces headlines along the lines of Professor Diesen “denies” spreading Russian propaganda or Professor Diesen “denies” being paid by the Kremlin. What is there to deny when there is never an argument or any evidence to address?

During the past 6.5 years, I have only once been asked for my opinion on a political issue, back in 2022. The newspaper was subsequently pressured by the mob into apologising and even published an article thereafter arguing that it should have informed the public that I was “controversial”. They had the opportunity to challenge my arguments during the live interview but did not. They never explained what I had said that was wrong, nor did they give me an opportunity to defend myself against their denunciation. Since then, even the Defence Minister cautioned the two podcasters against speaking with me as I was accused of spreading “Russian propaganda” by arguing (and documenting) that NATO expansion provoked the Ukraine War. So I ask again, what inquiries have I ever ignored? The journalists are eagerly shaping the narrative of my resignation, not reporting on reality.

The campaign after I resigned

I initially considered taking a temporary break and asked my university for one year of unpaid leave to get away physically and escape the headlines. As I wrote to my university, I requested “one year of unpaid research leave to conduct research within my core area of expertise, with the application further supported by additional circumstances, including death threats, harassment in the workplace, and other challenges that have made it necessary to withdraw my children from school and sell our house”. My application was rejected without any explanation and with no interest in even addressing the documented harassment in the workplace. After I was left with no other option but to submit my resignation from the university, I thought that at least we would get some peace by permanently ending my employment in Norway.

However, over the past week, no fewer than 15 Norwegian media outlets have published hit pieces about me, and not a single one could point to anything specific I have actually argued. Yet, there was no shortage of meaningless labels and citing of unsubstantiated smears. I am baffled by the intensity and absurdity of it all, especially since these articles are all based on reporting that I have already resigned from my position as a professor at the university.

They have already won… The endless smears, censorship, threats, and intimidation worked — yet they still do not stop. This new campaign seems intended merely to ensure that I leave the country completely discredited.

While it is extremely sad to be pushed out of the country and pressured into exile, I take some comfort in knowing that, in a few weeks, I can return to normal teaching and a normal life beyond this Norwegian bubble of warmongering, disinformation, and censorship where academic freedom goes to die.

item.title: Freedom of Speech Dies in a Europe Obsessed with Speaking as One
item.description: How can you have freedom of speech when Europe is obsessed with the idea of speaking with one voice?
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded: How can you have freedom of speech when Europe is obsessed with the idea of speaking with one voice? A united voice is established when politics is framed in the language of morality, where there can only be good and evil. The consequence of not allowing dissent? Academics who discuss the uncontroversial topic of NATO expansion undermining a pan-European security architecture and the principle of indivisible security are met with state-financed intimidation. Europe today has transitioned from liberal democracy to an ideological cult.
